approach: Nothing records which reading rule refused a reading, so the plan adds the smallest record field first. Each reader invocation whose output reached the reading rules gets an optional `reading_attempt` field: `attempt` is 1 for the first reading and 2 for the re-read, and `refusal` is `{rule, text}` or absent when the reading was accepted. `read_once` in reading.rs sets it. It switches from `check_reading_acceptance` to `refusing_check`, which already returns the name of the first refusing check and gives the same accept/refuse result and text. A size refusal (from `build_reading`) is named `check_reading_size`, and any other invalid reader output is named `other`. `status.rs` adds `ReadingRuleStats::compute(&Records)`. It takes the 50 most recent first readings (attempt-1 invocations by `started_at`), pairs each with its re-read (same job, seq+1), and counts per rule the first readings refused and the second readings still refused. It also keeps the most common first-refusal text per rule. `StatusView.reading_rules` carries it, `text()` prints it, and display.rs calls `text()`. hestia.rs adds a pure `reading_rule_findings(&ReadingRuleStats)` and a `ReadingRulesCheck` that implements `Check`. `hestia_sweep_with` (the real `athena hestia sweep` path) runs it next to the caller's checks. The check flags a rule only when its first-refusal count × 100 is greater than the first-reading count × `REFUSAL_FLAG_PERCENT` (30), and only when the window holds at least `MIN_FIRST_READINGS` (10) first readings. Below the minimum it reports `examined = 0` and no finding, and prints no "healthy" line. No reading rule, refusal text, prompt or governance file changes. There is no landing, history-check or attribution rule here, so no commit-shape table applies.

decisions.choice: Record the refusal as a typed optional field `reading_attempt: Option<ReadingAttempt{attempt, refusal: Option<ReadingRefusal{rule,text}>}>` on `Invocation` (`#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if)]`, schema stays `athena.invocation/1`), written on every reader invocation that reached the rules (accepted or refused).
decisions.reason: Nothing stores the refusal text or rule today. `read_once` returns it only as an in-memory `ReadError::Refused(String)`, and the Reading record exists only for an accepted reading. The Invocation is committed for both runs of `read_for` (`invocation_files`), including a double refusal that leaves no Reading. The field must be written on accepted attempts too: the denominator ('first readings') needs the accepted ones, and the `attempt` number separates a first reading from a re-read after `read_unread` (reading.rs:1051).

rejected.why: `detail` is free text that other code treats as a failure reason (reading.rs:668, hestia.rs:2342, steward.rs:1283). Overloading it needs prefix parsing and mixes failure and refusal meanings.

rejected.option: A new record type such as `athena.reading-refusal/1`
rejected.why: Needs a new `AnyRecord` variant, canonical path, schema and store loading. That is far larger than one optional field and still needs a link back to the invocation.
A double refusal leaves no Reading, and the first refusal of an accepted second reading would still need a place. The Reading also has many struct literals.

rejected.option: Count invocations per job only (a job with two reader invocations means a re-read)
rejected.why: This gives no rule and no text, which the request asks for. The brief says to measure the property directly, not through a stand-in.

decisions.choice: Name the rule with `refusing_check`'s returned check name (`stringify!` of the called function). A `check_reading_size` error is named `check_reading_size` by wrapping it at its call site in `build_reading` in a small error type whose Display is the unchanged text. Any other `build_reading` failure is `other` (`OTHER_READING_RULE`).
decisions.reason: `refusing_check` (checks.rs:518) is the one gate the refusal corpus pins, with names such as `check_scope_limit` and `check_governance_coverage` (refusal_corpus.rs:347, 842). No second list of rule names can drift. A downcast is exact, where text prefixes are fragile. The size rule stays untouched.

rejected.option: Map refusal text to a rule by prefix after the fact
rejected.why: A prefix table is a second list that drifts when a rule's wording changes. The name is known at refusal time.

rejected.option: Edit `check_reading_size` to return a typed error
rejected.why: Out of scope: the brief forbids changing a reading rule or its refusal text.

decisions.choice: The window is the 50 most recent first readings (attempt-1 invocations, ordered by `started_at`, then job id and seq) across all jobs. `READING_WINDOW = 50` is a named constant in status.rs. A second reading is the attempt-2 invocation of the same job with seq = first.seq + 1. A re-read after a user correction (reading.rs:1287) and a re-read after a failed reader (`read_unread`) each count as a reading.
decisions.reason: A job whose two readings were both refused has no Reading record, and those are the costliest cases, so 'jobs that have a reading' would hide them. Pairing by seq matches `read_for`, which uses `seq` and `seq + 1`. The brief's 'per job' wording is approximated per reading, and the plan says so in the docs and CHANGELOG.

rejected.option: Count only jobs that have a Reading record
rejected.why: It misses double refusals, so refusal rates would look better than they are.

decisions.choice: Each refusal names exactly one rule, because the gate stops at the first refusing check. The sweep rate for a rule is first refusals by that rule divided by first readings in the window. It is flagged only when `first_refused * 100 > first_readings * REFUSAL_FLAG_PERCENT` (`REFUSAL_FLAG_PERCENT = 30`), so exactly 30% is not flagged. No flag is made when the window has fewer than `MIN_FIRST_READINGS = 10` first readings.
decisions.reason: This follows the brief's 'more than 30%'. Integer arithmetic avoids float edge cases at exactly 30%. With fewer than 10 readings one refusal swings the rate by 10 points or more, and an empty window must not be read as healthy (the no-empty-success default).

rejected.option: Flag on any rate above 30% regardless of window size
rejected.why: One refused reading in a window of one is 100%, which would be a false flag.

rejected.option: Report 'healthy' when no rule is over the limit
rejected.why: The brief forbids a healthy claim for an empty or tiny window. The sweep adds no healthy text at all.

decisions.choice: The most common first-refusal text of a rule is the exact text with the highest count in the window. A tie goes to the most recent. The sweep evidence cuts it with the existing `one_line` (240 characters).
decisions.reason: The brief asks for 'most common refusal text'. Exact grouping is the plain reading of that phrase. Path-specific texts will often tie at 1, so the latest tie-break gives an example from the newest reading.

rejected.option: Normalise text into templates before grouping
rejected.why: It would be a new matching rule with its own failure shapes. Not needed to meet the criteria.

decisions.choice: Run the new check from `hestia_sweep_with` by splitting the measuring pass out of `hestia_sweep_measuring` and committing the sweep over the caller's checks plus the reading-rule check. `hestia_sweep`, `hestia_sweep_measuring` and `default_checks()` keep their behavior.
decisions.reason: `Check::run(now)` has no records, so the check is built from `ReadingRuleStats`, computed with `Records::load_current` as `status()` does. The existing tests assert `default_checks().is_empty()` (hestia.rs:2868), two checks in a `hestia_sweep` record (hestia.rs:2949) and exactly 3 ui lines per `hestia_sweep_with` (hestia.rs:4728). Adding no ui line and not touching `hestia_sweep` keeps all three true.

rejected.why: It has no access to records, and a test pins it empty.
That changes the check count that tests at hestia.rs:2936-2950 and 4591-4687 rely on.

rejected.option: Print a 'not enough readings' ui line
rejected.why: It would raise the pinned line count (hestia.rs:4728), and the record already shows `examined` 0 and 0 findings.

decisions.choice: List only rules that refused at least once in the window. Do not keep a constant list of all rule names.
decisions.reason: The refusal-rate question is about rules that cause re-reads. A full list would be a second copy of the `step!` lines, with a drift test to maintain. The window totals are always printed, so a rule absent from the list refused nothing in the window.

rejected.why: Adds a list that must stay in step with `refusing_check`, for no extra decision.

risks.risk: The gate stops at the first refusing check, so a rule later in the order is hidden whenever an earlier rule refuses the same reading. Its rate can be understated.
risks.mitigation: The measure is documented as refusals by the first rule to refuse, which is also what triggers the re-read. No rule order or text changes.

risks.risk: Refusal texts name request-specific paths, so exact-text grouping often ties at 1 and 'most common text' is only an example.
risks.mitigation: A tie goes to the most recent text, the sweep evidence shows its count, and the status test pins that rule.

risks.risk: Older records have no `reading_attempt`, so the window is thin right after the change and the sweep stays silent.
risks.mitigation: The minimum of 10 first readings means no flag and no healthy claim. `examined` stays 0 in the sweep record.

risks.risk: An older installed binary rejects new invocation records because of `deny_unknown_fields`.
risks.mitigation: The field is serialized only on reader invocations that reached the rules. The existing stale-build warning covers old binaries, and new binaries read old records through `#[serde(default)]`.

risks.risk: Redaction: the refusal text can quote request or reading text.
risks.mitigation: `read_once` passes the text through `redactor.redact_all` before storing it, as `build_reading` does for other reader free text.

risks.risk: hestia.rs and status.rs are very large files and function size is tracked by code-health.
risks.mitigation: New code is small, separate functions, none long, and the `hestia_sweep_with` refactor only moves the existing measuring-pass match into a helper.

risks.risk: The CLI printing is a one-line call to `text()`, which has no test through the `athena status` binary.
risks.mitigation: `text()` is tested in status.rs and the label test checks the `"readings ` literal exists. The `Option` stays absent when empty, as the existing introspection.rs status tests already check for `gate_counts`.

The full-path test shows the committed sweep for the backlog fixture of the existing test (hestia.rs:4693) has the check with count 0 and examined 0.
demonstrations.fails_without: Without the minimum, 9 all-refused readings would flag. Reporting `examined` as 9 with 0 findings would let a reader take a tiny window as healthy.

demonstrations.method: Add tests in athena-data records.rs for the new field. One test makes a full Invocation fixture with `reading_attempt` set, both accepted and refused. It round-trips through `AnyRecord::Invocation(..).to_json()` and `AnyRecord::parse`, and `check_record_file` accepts it at its `canonical_path()`. One test shows an Invocation JSON without the field parses with `None`, and an unknown key inside `reading_attempt` is rejected (`deny_unknown_fields`).
demonstrations.observes: The round trip returns an equal record. `check_record_file(path, bytes)` returns `Ok(Some(AnyRecord::Invocation(..)))` and a misplaced path is `Misplaced`. Old records still parse.
demonstrations.fails_without: Without `#[serde(default)]` an old record fails to parse. Without the field on the struct, the round trip would drop the refusal.
